title: Why Temporal

story: Monday, 09:00. You assign RH-1234 to Nova, and by 09:25 Nova has a plan for the "No projects yet" card and posts it for you to approve. But you left for a long weekend at 09:10, so the plan waits. You press Approve on Thursday morning, Nova builds for 70 minutes, asks one question and opens the PR in the afternoon.

Between Monday and Thursday the orchestrator, the service that runs every agent run, is deployed four times, and one of its machines crashes. If the run lived in the memory of a Node process, as a variable that holds the plan and a setTimeout for the reminder, the first deploy would erase it. Nobody would know until you asked why nothing happened to your ticket.
hook.question: How can one function run for three days when the process that runs it restarts several times on the way?

read.h: A function that outlives its process
p: Think about how you would build this without help. The plan, the decision and the current step would go into a database table, because memory dies with the process. A cron job would look for runs that should continue and continue them. You would add retries around every call to Jira and Slack, a lock so that two machines never continue the same run, and a table of timers for the reminders. That is a lot of code, and every bug in it loses somebody's ticket.

Temporal is that code, written once and used by many teams. You write the run as one ordinary async function, and Temporal makes sure it finishes even when the machines under it do not. The name for this is durable execution: the progress of the function is stored outside the process, so another process can continue it. Here is the run for a ticket, cut down to three steps.

The function is called a workflow. A workflow decides what happens and in which order. The two functions it calls, writePlan and openPr, are activities: an activity does one piece of outside work, such as claiming a VM, posting to Slack or reading a ticket. The workflow may wait between steps for a second or for three days, and while it waits, none of your code runs at all.

notes.text: Only the types of the activities are imported. The workflow never runs activity code itself.
proxyActivities gives back stand-ins. Calling one asks Temporal to run the real activity on a worker and waits for its result.
A durable timer. The Temporal Service keeps it, not your process, so the process may die while it waits.

p: Three things are involved: the Temporal Service, a worker and a client. The Temporal Service is a server with a database. It stores what happened in every run, and it holds task queues, which are named lists of work waiting to be done. It never runs your code. A worker is your own Node process: it connects to the service, keeps asking one task queue for work, and runs your workflow and activity code when work arrives. A client is any code that starts a run or sends one a message; for us that is the Jira poll and the Slack app.

Now the flow. The Jira poll, as a client, asks the service to start ticketToPr with the ID nova:RH-1234. The service records the start and puts a task on the queue ai-agents-nova. A worker that listens on that queue takes the task and runs the function until the first await, where the workflow asks for writePlan. That request goes onto the queue as well, a worker runs writePlan, and its result is recorded. Then the workflow reaches the sleep, and the worker has nothing to do for this run until the timer fires.

notes.text: The worker only takes work from this queue. A run started on another queue never reaches it.
Workflow code is given as a file, because the worker bundles it and runs it in a sandbox: a closed space inside the worker with no network and no Node modules.
Activities are given as plain functions and run as normal Node code, with full access to the network.

p: Every run has an event history: the list of facts the service recorded for it, in order. You can print it with the temporal CLI. This is nova:RH-1234 from the lab, printed while the worker was stopped in the middle of the sleep.

Say the worker crashes during the sleep. The timer still fires, because the service keeps it. A new worker gets the next task for this run, but it has nothing in memory, so it does a replay: it runs ticketToPr again from the top. At await writePlan(ticket) it finds ActivityTaskCompleted in the history and returns the recorded result at once, without running writePlan. At the sleep it finds TimerFired and moves on. At openPr there is no record yet, so from here on the work is real. The function is back where it was, with the same plan in the same variable, and nothing ran twice.
read.see:
$ temporal workflow show -w nova:RH-1234      (worker stopped during the sleep)
    1  WorkflowExecutionStarted
    5  ActivityTaskScheduled
    7  ActivityTaskCompleted     ← writePlan's result, stored
   11  TimerStarted              ← the sleep, kept by the service
(trimmed: the WorkflowTask… lines are the worker taking its turns)

deeper.h: Go deeper: replay is the exception, not the rule
p: A worker keeps the runs it is working on in memory, in a cache, so in normal operation it does not replay a whole history for every step: it continues the function from where it stopped. Replay happens when the run's worker is gone, or when the cache is full and the run was pushed out.

That is also why the lab may show a WorkflowTaskTimedOut event after you restart the worker. Temporal first offered the next task to the worker that had the run in memory, waited about ten seconds for it, and then gave the task to any worker on the queue.

read.h: The rule that replay depends on
p: Replay only works if the workflow makes the same calls in the same order every time it runs. If the workflow read a file or called an API itself, a replay three days later could get a different answer and take a different path, and the history would no longer match the code. So everything that touches the outside world goes into an activity, where it runs once and its result is recorded. In other words, workflow code must be deterministic: given the same history, it always does the same thing.

The TypeScript SDK helps you keep this rule. Inside the workflow sandbox there is no fetch and no Node module, so the mistake fails at once instead of silently. Date.now() and Math.random() still work, but the SDK replaces them: the time is the time recorded for the current step, and the random numbers come from a seed stored with the run, so a replay gets the same values. In the lab you break this rule on purpose and see what Temporal does.

lab.title: Kill the worker in the middle of a run
needs: About 250 MB of disk for the Temporal packages
lab.goal: Stop the worker while a run sleeps, start it again, and see the run finish without repeating the step it already did.

guess.q: The run has finished writePlan and is in its 30-second sleep. You stop the worker with Ctrl+C and start it again after the 30 seconds. The new worker runs ticketToPr from the top. Does "writePlan ran for RH-1234" appear a second time?

options.text: Yes, because the new worker runs the whole function again from the first line.
options.why: It does run the function from the top, but the call to writePlan is answered from the history, so the activity itself does not run.

options.text: No. writePlan's result comes from the history, and only openPr really runs.
options.why: That is replay: recorded steps return their saved result, and only steps with no record do real work.

options.text: Nothing appears, because the run died with the worker and must be started again.
options.why: The run lives in the Temporal Service, not in the worker. The timer fires on the service and waits for any worker to come back.

follow.say: Start a Temporal Service on your laptop in the first tab and leave it open. It keeps everything in memory, which is fine for a lab.

follow.say: Write the two activities. Each one prints a line, so you can see exactly when it really runs.
Write the workflow. It calls writePlan, sleeps for 30 seconds (the stand-in for three days) and then calls openPr.
Write the worker, which runs the code, and a small client that starts one run named after the ticket.
Start the worker in the second tab and leave it running.
follow.see: Worker is running. Ctrl+C stops it.

(in the worker tab)

lab.build: Add a third activity, askForReview(pr), that prints "askForReview ran for <pr>" and returns "review requested from the frontend team". Call it after openPr and return its result as part of the workflow's result. Restart the worker, because it bundles the workflow code only when it starts. Then start a run for another ticket with node start.mjs RH-1235, stop the worker during the sleep, start it again after 30 seconds, and check the history.
checks: After the restart, the worker prints "openPr ran for RH-1234", and "writePlan ran for RH-1234" appears only once in the whole lab.
temporal workflow result -w nova:RH-1234 shows Status COMPLETED.
In temporal workflow show -w nova:RH-1234, TimerStarted and TimerFired sit between the two ActivityTaskCompleted events.
For your build: temporal workflow show -w nova:RH-1235 | grep -c ActivityTaskCompleted prints 3, and the result ends with "review requested from the frontend team".
lab.fix: A teammate wanted Slack to hear about the plan as soon as it is written, so they added one line to the workflow, right after writePlan: await fetch('https://slack.com/api/chat.postMessage', { method: 'POST', body: plan }). Add that line, restart the worker and run node start.mjs RH-1300. The run stays Running forever, and the worker prints ReferenceError: fetch is not defined again and again. Repair it by moving the Slack call into a new activity, postPlan, and calling that from the workflow. Then clean up the stuck run with temporal workflow terminate -w nova:RH-1300.
explain: The worker was gone for 30 seconds, but the run still finished. Where was the run during that time, and where was the timer?
Why did writePlan not run again after the restart, even though the new worker ran ticketToPr from the first line?
Why does a call to Slack belong in an activity and not in the workflow, even though both are async functions?
lab.done: The run nova:RH-1234 completed after you killed and restarted the worker, writePlan ran only once, and you stopped the worker and the dev server with Ctrl+C.

check.q: The worker is killed while the run sleeps. After a new worker starts, what happens to the writePlan call at the top of the function?

options.text: It runs again, because the new worker starts the function from the first line
options.why: The function does start from the first line, but the call is answered from the history. The activity itself does not run.

options.text: Its result is read from the history, so writePlan does not run again
options.why: That is replay. Steps with a record return the saved result, and only steps without one do real work.

options.text: The run fails and someone has to start it again
options.why: Nothing is lost. The run and its timer live in the Temporal Service, which waits for any worker to come back.

check.q: A teammate wants the workflow to read the ticket from Jira itself, "because the workflow is async anyway". What is wrong with that?

options.text: Nothing, as long as the call is wrapped in try and catch
options.why: Error handling does not help. The problem is that a replay would make the call again and could get a different answer.

options.text: It is only slower, because activities are faster than workflow code
options.why: Speed is not the problem. Determinism is: the workflow must make the same decisions every time it replays.

options.text: On a replay the call would run again and could return something new, so the workflow could take a path that does not match its history
options.why: Outside calls go in activities, which run once and are recorded. In TypeScript the sandbox even refuses: fetch is not defined in workflow code.

check.q: What does the Temporal Service do while nova:RH-1234 waits three days for approval?

options.text: It keeps the run's history and its timer, and hands the next task to a worker when something happens
options.why: The service stores and hands out work. Your code only runs in workers, and only when there is a task.

options.text: It runs the workflow function in a loop, checking every second whether the approval came
options.why: The service never runs your code. While the run waits, no code runs at all.

options.text: It keeps Nova's VM and Claude session alive until the approval comes
options.why: Temporal does not run the agent. The VM is released while a person thinks, and the wait costs nothing.

p: Our own Temporal Service runs on our infra cluster, inf, with a Temporal namespace called ai-agents that keeps the history of every run for 30 days. Its web UI is only reachable over the VPN or Teleport. The orchestrator is the set of workers that run our workflows: ticketToPr for Nova, routineRun for the routines, and a few small housekeeping workflows.

Temporal does not run the agent. Nova runs in the harness on a sandbox VM; the workflow only claims the VM, starts the harness, watches it and releases the VM, each through an activity. That split is why a three-day wait costs nothing: while a person thinks, no VM runs and no workflow code runs.

tickets.why: Runs our own Temporal Service on inf, with the namespace ai-agents and its search attributes.
ticketToPr is one workflow whose long waits only work because Temporal keeps the run alive.
Runs live for days, so every deploy lands in the middle of some run; replay is what makes that safe.

words.plain: Running a function whose progress is stored outside the process, so another process can continue it after a crash.
The function that decides what happens in a run and in which order. It must be deterministic.
A function that does one piece of outside work. It runs once and its result is recorded.
Your own process that asks a task queue for work and runs workflow and activity code.
The list of facts the Temporal Service recorded for one run, in order.
Running the workflow again from the top and answering every recorded step from the history.

review.q: Name the three parts of a Temporal setup and say in one sentence what each does.
review.a: The Temporal Service stores histories and task queues and never runs code; a worker is your process that runs workflow and activity code from a queue; a client starts runs and sends them messages.

review.q: A new worker replays a run that already finished two activities and a timer. What does it do at each of those three awaits?
review.a: It returns the recorded results of the two activities and moves past the fired timer without waiting, so nothing runs twice; real work starts at the first step with no record.

review.q: Why must all outside work be in activities?
review.a: A workflow is replayed from its history, so it must decide the same way every time. An outside call could answer differently on replay; an activity runs once and its result is recorded.

remember: The workflow decides and is replayed from its history; activities do the outside work once, and their results are recorded.
